lessons.title: Track the actor and the object
lessons.explanation: Earlier you requested water with a noun that differed from its dictionary form. Now make that pattern productive. The objective is to distinguish the participant doing an action from the thing directly affected by it. Start with Книга (KNEE-ga) — book; dictionary form. In a reading statement, use Я читаю книгу (ya chee-TA-yu KNEE-gu) — I am reading a book / I read a book. The book remains the same object in the world, but its ending tells the listener how the noun participates in the sentence. A case is not a new species of book or a change in its physical properties. It is a grammatical form associated with a role. Learn a reliable small pattern before attempting a complete table of endings.
lessons.example: Suppose a friend asks what you are doing, and you have a book open. Select yourself as the actor, select the present reading verb, and place the book in the direct-object role: Я читаю книгу (ya chee-TA-yu KNEE-gu) — I am reading a book / I read a book. The noun's dictionary ending represented by -a becomes -u in this construction. That noun change does not alter the tense. It also does not say that you finished reading. Translate the entire proposition rather than assigning a separate English word to every ending. Read the item slowly, preserving the stressed syllables; then join the words at a comfortable natural pace without forcing speed.

depth.definitions: The subject is the grammatical participant with which the finite verb normally agrees; here it is also the actor. A direct object is a participant selected directly by a transitive verb: here, the thing read. Transitive means that the verb can take a direct object. Nominative names the subject or dictionary form used here; accusative names the direct-object case used here. These definitions are starting points: not every subject is an intentional actor, and not every accusative phrase is a direct object. English preserves comparable pronoun contrasts in he versus him, even though ordinary nouns seldom change this way. Pronunciation key: capitals mark stressed syllables, hyphens divide convenient sound chunks, sh and zh approximate the corresponding hushing consonants, and kh is a breathy sound like Spanish j. The cue y after a consonant sometimes represents a Russian central vowel, not English ee. These Latin guides are approximate scaffolds, not phonetic transcriptions; use the item audio to hear soft consonants and unstressed vowels.
depth.mechanism: Make two decisions: function first, form second. Determine that the book is the object of reading, then retrieve the accusative singular appropriate to its noun pattern. Cornell explicitly separates what a case does from what its endings look and sound like.[1] For this regular -a noun, the accusative ending is -u.[2] But the rule is not “all objects end in -u.” Compare Я читаю журнал (ya chee-TA-yu zhoor-NAL) — I am reading a magazine / I read a magazine. This masculine inanimate noun has the same visible nominative and accusative form. A grammatical contrast need not have a unique visible ending in every word. Word order provides additional clues and helps organize old and new information. Keep neutral actor–verb–object order for these first productions rather than treating flexible Russian word order as random permutation.
depth.secondExample: Imagine two pictures: one reader holds a book and another holds a magazine. The corresponding captions are Я читаю книгу (ya chee-TA-yu KNEE-gu) — I am reading a book / I read a book and Я читаю журнал (ya chee-TA-yu zhoor-NAL) — I am reading a magazine / I read a magazine. Both nouns are accusative objects even though only the book visibly changes. The distinction is noun pattern, not whether magazines count as real objects. Spanish articles can make gender especially visible; Russian does not have a matching article in these sentences. Do not invent an extra word to represent English a or the. Context can tell listeners whether a particular book is meant. Some differences between languages concern what they leave unspecified, not what they fail to express.
depth.mistake: A predictable error copies the dictionary book form unchanged because English book remains book. Diagnose this by labeling actor, action, and object before correcting the ending. Another error adds -u to the magazine noun, overextending a genuine pattern. Place both model sentences on the same study card: one grammatical role, two surface patterns. If you identify the role correctly but hesitate over the form, record a retrieval gap rather than concluding that you understand nothing. Conversely, an accurately memorized sentence is not yet evidence that you can choose its form in a new situation.
depth.application: Optional practice: draw the two objects and produce one reading caption for each. Explain in English why only one noun visibly changes. Model response: both nouns are direct objects and accusative, but this book noun changes its ending whereas this masculine inanimate magazine noun does not. Self-review checks four features: actor, reading verb, correct object form, and no unsupported claim of finishing. Use each item's Slow and Natural controls when integrated; compare the stressed syllables rather than demanding accent imitation. If you prefer not to record speech, point to the forms and explain the distinction aloud. The activity is nonblocking and can be repeated later.
depth.summary: Case connects sentence role with word form. Preserve the distinction between assigning a case and spelling it. Next, the same library noun will represent either a location or a destination, showing that one case can serve more than one function.

lessons.question: Why can two direct objects have different-looking endings?
lessons.answer: Their noun patterns realize the accusative differently.
lessons.distractor: Every object must visibly end in -u.
lessons.correction: Assign role first; retrieve the form according to noun class.

lessons.title: Separate location from destination
lessons.explanation: The objective is to tell someone where you are and where you are going without confusing the two relations. Earlier you asked where the metro was and learned a going-home phrase. Compare Я в библиотеке (ya v beeb-lee-a-TYE-kye) — I am in the library with Я иду в библиотеку (ya ee-DOO v beeb-lee-a-TYE-ku) — I am going to the library on foot. The building is the same, and the short preposition is the same, but the noun ending differs. One sentence places you inside a setting; the other identifies the goal of a walking journey. English often signals this difference with in versus to. Russian can retain its preposition and change the following noun's case. Translating relationships is therefore more reliable than substituting words individually.
lessons.example: A friend calls while you are among the library shelves. Ask which relationship you need: a current location, not a path. Choose Я в библиотеке (ya v beeb-lee-a-TYE-kye) — I am in the library. This present location statement normally has no overt equivalent of English am. On another day you leave home and tell your friend your immediate goal: Я иду в библиотеку (ya ee-DOO v beeb-lee-a-TYE-ku) — I am going to the library on foot. The walking verb supplies the action, and the destination uses accusative. The library is not a direct object that you read or carry; the preposition and directional meaning license this accusative. The case has more than one function, so it should not be memorized as a single English word.

depth.definitions: Location answers Где? (GDYE) — where?; location. Destination answers Куда? (ku-DA) — where to?; destination. The prepositional case is used after certain prepositions; here it marks location after the preposition meaning in. A preposition is a small word expressing a relationship with the phrase that follows. Government means that a word or construction requires a grammatical form, not political control. The destination construction governs accusative; the location construction here governs prepositional. Learn the two library forms together rather than generalizing their spelling immediately to every other noun. Names for forms help organize the evidence, but the communicative relationship should remain your first decision.
depth.mechanism: Cornell contrasts location with directed motion through the cases following the same prepositions.[3] A useful diagnostic is to ask whether the library describes where an activity happens or where a path leads. The mere presence of a motion verb is insufficient. A person can walk around inside a library, making it the setting of motion rather than its destination. Conversely, a planned destination can be named before anyone moves. Thus “motion always means accusative” is an unreliable shortcut. The supplied going sentence concerns a directed journey on foot, not every form of travel. A destination also does not assert arrival: someone can change plans halfway. Grammar identifies the kind of relationship being represented, not whether the journey succeeds.
depth.secondExample: A text message is supposed to update a friend's knowledge of your whereabouts. If you remain at home preparing to leave, a contextually appropriate going-to-library statement can express your immediate plan; the in-the-library statement would misrepresent your present location. Once you arrive, the latter becomes an accurate answer to the location question. Translate both back into English and identify their limits. The location sentence does not explain how you arrived; the destination sentence does not establish that you are already there. Neither sentence is defective simply because it leaves those matters open.
depth.mistake: A common error keeps the library form unchanged because the preposition looks the same in both sentences. Treat preposition plus case as a meaningful combination. Another error extends the familiar location ending to every noun. This lesson supplies a dependable library pair, not a complete algorithm for all declensions. Unknown nouns may have different endings or stress patterns. A third error adds a present equivalent of am because English requires one. The location model is already a complete ordinary Russian sentence; resist repairing it according to English syntax.
depth.application: Optional practice: draw one person inside a building and another on an arrow toward it. Match the supplied full sentences to the drawings. Model reasoning: the inside panel requires location and the learned prepositional form; the arrow panel requires a goal and the learned accusative form. Check relationship, noun form, verb presence, and truthfulness. Then shorten the arrow so it stops halfway and explain why arrival is still not established. As a transfer task, describe in English a person walking inside the building and explain why movement alone does not decide which case the setting needs. You may continue after the answer review.
depth.summary: Choose a relationship before choosing a case. The same place can be a setting or a goal, and its form follows the construction. Next you will describe the absence of a resource rather than the location of a person.

lessons.question: What does naming a destination fail to establish?
lessons.answer: That the traveler has already arrived.
lessons.distractor: That the destination is a goal.
lessons.correction: A goal can be identified while the journey remains incomplete.

lessons.title: Express missing resources with the genitive
lessons.explanation: Your earlier possession formula can become a useful statement about absence. Compare У меня есть книга (u mee-NYA YEST KNEE-ga) — I have a book with У меня нет книги (u mee-NYA NYET KNEE-gee) — I do not have a book. Do not simply negate an English have while leaving all Russian forms unchanged. The negative-existence construction requires the missing thing in the genitive case. The objective is to distinguish lacking a resource from not performing an action with it, and to retrieve reliable forms for two useful resources. The book does not become a different object when its ending changes. Its role in a different construction explains the form. Learn the affirmative and negative sentences as a meaningful contrast rather than a collection of unrelated phrases.
lessons.example: You and a partner are preparing to read. If a book is available to you, use У меня есть книга (u mee-NYA YEST KNEE-ga) — I have a book. If none is available, use У меня нет книги (u mee-NYA NYET KNEE-gee) — I do not have a book. Work outward from the central relationship: there is an absence; the book identifies what is absent; the opening phrase places that absence in your sphere of possession. I do not have a book is natural English. The rough literal structure “at me there is no book” can reveal the grammar but is not a polished translation. Depending on context, having may concern ownership or present availability. Someone can own a book and still lack one at the current meeting.

depth.definitions: Genitive names a case with several functions, including relationships involving possession, quantity, and absence. Those functions occur in different constructions and should not be collapsed into one rule. Existence concerns whether something is present in a relevant domain. A possessor phrase can attach that existence claim to a person. A noun pattern supplies the forms appropriate to each construction. Book and time do not share a complete set of endings merely because both can name missing resources. The term impersonal describes a construction without an ordinary nominative subject of the sort found in our reading sentence.
depth.mechanism: Cornell presents this negative construction as impersonal and marks the missing item with genitive.[4] Remove the explicit possessor and you get Нет книги (NYET KNEE-gee) — There is no book. Context must now establish the relevant setting: perhaps a bag, a desk, or a study meeting. This does not assert that no books exist anywhere. Everyday language routinely restricts claims to an understood situation. Also separate absence from action negation: lacking a book does not prevent reading an electronic text, while not reading says nothing about owning books. Russian has additional rules for objects under negated verbs, but those are not prerequisites for this clear absence construction. A single English negative word is not sufficient evidence for selecting genitive throughout an entire Russian sentence.
depth.secondExample: A study invitation may encounter a different problem: У меня нет времени (u mee-NYA NYET VRYE-mee-nee) — I do not have time. Time is the missing resource. Learn the phrase as a reliable unit rather than inventing its form by copying the book ending. It means you have no available time in this context, not that physical time has ceased to exist. The practical implications differ: lacking a book invites an offer to lend one; lacking time invites rescheduling. The grammar packages both as absence, but communication depends on what is missing. A listener needs the noun's meaning, not only the correct case label, to respond helpfully.
depth.mistake: The most likely form error retains the affirmative book form after the negative expression. Label the intended construction before repairing the ending: this is absence, not affirmative possession. Pair the two full sentences in practice. A more serious conceptual error calls genitive “the negative case” and applies it wherever an English translation contains not. Correct that by naming the limited construction explicitly. Another misunderstanding interprets lack of a resource as dislike of the activity. Nothing in the time or book sentence states a preference, so avoid adding that inference when translating.
depth.application: Optional practice: give two different replies to a study invitation, one for unavailable books and one for unavailable time. Explain what practical solution each suggests. Model response: the first makes borrowing relevant; the second makes scheduling relevant. Self-review checks the intended resource, its learned genitive form, the possessor phrase, and absence of invented claims about motivation. For a deeper check, remove the possessor from the book sentence and describe what additional context a listener would need. You may explain in English first, then speak the Russian model. This separates conceptual reasoning from pronunciation retrieval and makes your next practice target easier to identify.
depth.summary: A negative-existence construction selects the missing resource's form. Keep the domain, absence, and resource distinct. Next add a recipient to an action and learn why a person receiving a book is not the same grammatical participant as the book itself.

lessons.answer: The absent resource takes genitive in this construction.
lessons.distractor: Every noun in every negative sentence must be genitive.
lessons.correction: The local construction determines the case; English negation alone does not.

lessons.title: Give an object to a recipient
lessons.explanation: A giving event contains more than one participant after the actor. The objective is to distinguish the transferred object from its recipient. Use Я даю книгу Анне (ya da-YU KNEE-gu AN-nye) — I am giving a book to Anna. The book is what changes hands; Anna receives it. Russian uses dative for this recipient. English can say give Anna a book or give a book to Anna, placing the same relation in different word orders. Do not infer from English position that Anna and book have identical Russian grammar. Analyze what each participant contributes to the event. Your earlier direct-object work remains useful: a new case adds another relationship rather than replacing the accusative everywhere.
lessons.example: Imagine physically passing a book to Anna. Start with the giver, yourself. Choose the giving verb. Identify the thing given and retrieve the accusative book form. Finally identify to whom it is given and select Anna's dative form: Я даю книгу Анне (ya da-YU KNEE-gu AN-nye) — I am giving a book to Anna. Each form answers a different question. Saying the sentence slowly may help you attach endings to roles, but avoid treating every word as an isolated puzzle when speaking naturally. The supplied verb presents giving as a current action or a general activity in an appropriate context; it is not a special claim that the transfer has already been completed.

depth.definitions: A recipient receives an object or communication. An addressee is the person to whom a message is directed. Dative names the case used for that participant in these models. Indirect object is a traditional grammatical term often associated with such roles, though its definition and distribution vary across languages. Valency describes the participants a verb can or must combine with. Giving can involve giver, thing given, and recipient; writing can mention a text, an addressee, both, or neither when context fills the gaps. The dictionary name Анна (AN-na) — Anna; dictionary/subject form can appear in different forms without naming different people.
depth.mechanism: Learn verbs together with their participant patterns. Cornell lists giving and writing among verbs that take dative and cautions against assuming exact English equivalence.[5] Thus Я пишу Анне (ya pee-SHOO AN-nye) — I am writing to Anna uses dative even without a physical object passing between people at that moment. The message need not be named. Dative is also not a mechanical translation of every English to. A library destination from the previous lesson used a preposition and accusative, because a goal of motion is not the same relation as a recipient. Personhood alone cannot determine the case either: the same person can be subject, object, recipient, or companion in different constructions. Word order is one clue, but the verb pattern and noun forms are more dependable than simply counting positions.
depth.secondExample: Now compare Я даю Анне журнал (ya da-YU AN-nye zhoor-NAL) — I am giving Anna a magazine. Anna appears before the magazine, whereas in the first example she followed the book. The roles remain recoverable: the magazine is transferred and Anna receives it. Order may change emphasis or what sounds like new information. In a conversation already about Anna, a final magazine noun can naturally supply the new point. This is information structure: the organization of a message around what is known and what is being added. It does not mean any word order is equally natural. For your own first productions, retain a model order until a conversational context motivates a change.
depth.mistake: One error calls Anna a direct object solely because English can put her immediately after give. Another assigns all postverbal nouns the book's accusative pattern. Repair both by sketching an arrow: the object moves toward the recipient. A third error inserts the library destination preposition before Anna because English says to. Correct that by recovering the full giving pattern, not by declaring that Russian recipients never use prepositions in any construction. The reliable local rule is that this giving recipient is dative without an added destination preposition.
depth.application: Optional practice: describe one transfer and one act of writing using the supplied models. Name the object and recipient wherever each is expressed. Model explanation: the book is accusative in the transfer, Anna is dative in both examples, and the writing sentence leaves the message unspecified. Self-review checks correct role labels, Anna's learned form, an appropriate action, and no claim that Anna is the thing being written. Extend the task by explaining why replacing Anna with library in the same structure does not automatically produce the earlier going-to-library sentence. You must choose a construction that matches motion rather than transfer or communication.
depth.summary: Verbs organize participants. Keep what is given separate from who receives it, even when word order changes. In the next lesson, add a tool and distinguish using an object from being accompanied by a person.

lessons.title: Use a tool and name a companion
lessons.explanation: English with can describe several relationships. Writing with a pen uses an implement; walking with Anna involves a companion. The objective is to preserve those different meanings in Russian rather than copying one English preposition. Compare Я пишу ручкой (ya pee-SHOO ROOCH-kay) — I am writing with a pen and Я иду с Анной (ya ee-DOO s AN-nay) — I am going on foot with Anna. The implement is instrumental without a preposition meaning with; accompaniment uses a preposition plus instrumental. Both constructions involve the same case name but not the same syntax. This lesson finishes a small network of roles rather than every possible case function. You can now distinguish objects, settings, destinations, absent resources, recipients, tools, and companions.
lessons.example: Suppose someone asks how you are producing a handwritten message. Choose writing as the action and a pen as the implement: Я пишу ручкой (ya pee-SHOO ROOCH-kay) — I am writing with a pen. The dictionary noun Ручка (ROOCH-ka) — pen; dictionary form has the instrumental form heard in the sentence. Do not automatically insert the preposition from the companion example. On leaving the library alongside Anna, use Я иду с Анной (ya ee-DOO s AN-nay) — I am going on foot with Anna. Anna participates beside you; she is not an implement used to perform walking. The choice begins with meaning and then selects grammar. This is a useful habit whenever one familiar English word has several possible Russian equivalents or constructions.

depth.definitions: Instrumental names the case associated here with a means and with accompaniment after a particular preposition. Means concerns how an action is carried out; accompaniment concerns someone or something participating alongside another. A construction pairs a form pattern with an interpretation. Bare instrumental for the pen is therefore distinct from preposition-plus-instrumental for the companion. The endings in these supplied singular examples are approximated as -ay in the pronunciation guide. That is a practical sound cue, not a universal rule covering every instrumental noun, gender, number, or stress pattern. Keep the complete models available as evidence.
depth.mechanism: Cornell explicitly warns English speakers not to insert the accompaniment preposition when an instrumental noun identifies a tool.[6] Translation must preserve relations rather than merely matching individual words. A recipient and implement can coexist: Я пишу Анне ручкой (ya pee-SHOO AN-nye ROOCH-kay) — I am writing to Anna with a pen. Anna answers to whom you write, while the pen answers what you use. The action remains writing but now has two distinct associated phrases. No noun's case follows simply from its distance from the verb. Instrumental also has other uses in more advanced constructions, so calling it only “the tool case” would become misleading. Treat these examples as stable islands from which to expand, while recognizing that a case's broader distribution cannot be reduced to one English preposition.
depth.secondExample: Draw two scenes. In the first, a message travels toward Anna while a pen touches the writer's paper. The expanded writing model fits. In the second, two people walk beside each other toward a library. The walking-with-Anna model fits. In the first scene Anna is a recipient; in the second she is a companion. People do not have one permanent grammatical case. Their relationship to a particular event determines the form. Similarly, a pen could be the thing given in another sentence rather than the means of writing. A semantic role belongs to the construction, not permanently to an object.
depth.mistake: A learner can retrieve an instrumental ending correctly yet still choose the wrong construction. Keep form errors and construction errors separate. A form error concerns the noun's shape; a construction error concerns the pattern in which that form occurs. Inserting the companion preposition into our pen-tool model is the latter. Another error assumes that every English with must share one Russian translation. Repair the assumption by paraphrasing English more precisely: using a pen versus accompanied by Anna. Those paraphrases reveal information hidden by the short preposition and make the Russian choice more intelligible.
depth.application: Optional unit project: sketch a study scene and describe reading a book, being in the library, and writing to Anna with a pen using this unit's models. Add a departure scene with Anna as companion. Model commentary: book is a direct object, library a setting, Anna a recipient in writing and companion in walking, and pen an implement. Self-review checks each relationship, its supplied form, and whether the scene supports the claim. Pronunciation review should preserve stress and intelligibility rather than reward imitation of an accent. If you know the form but forget the case name, record a terminology gap instead of treating successful communication as failure.
depth.summary: Choose the relationship, choose the construction, then retrieve its forms. The unit quiz samples those decisions in new scenarios, not unrestricted fluency. The next unit places activities and results in time so that these participants can appear in connected accounts.

units.title: Journeys, activities, and results across time

lessons.title: One journey or a repeated walking routine
lessons.explanation: You can distinguish a library location from a library destination. Now distinguish one directed journey from a recurring routine. Compare Я иду в библиотеку (ya ee-DOO v beeb-lee-a-TYE-ku) — I am going to the library on foot and Я хожу в библиотеку (ya ha-ZHOO v beeb-lee-a-TYE-ku) — I go to the library regularly. The destination phrase remains the same, while the verb changes the way the motion is presented. English go does not consistently reveal this difference on its own. The objective is to select an appropriate supplied walking model for a live travel update or a statement of habit. This distinction concerns motion pattern, not the importance of the destination or certainty of success. Learn to ask separate questions rather than seeking one ending that encodes everything.
lessons.example: A friend calls while you are walking toward the library. Give the live update Я иду в библиотеку (ya ee-DOO v beeb-lee-a-TYE-ku) — I am going to the library on foot. You present one directed journey. Later someone asks about your study routine rather than your whereabouts. Reply Я хожу в библиотеку (ya ha-ZHOO v beeb-lee-a-TYE-ku) — I go to the library regularly. In that context you describe repeated visits, and you may be sitting at home when you speak. The accusative destination remains appropriate in both models because library is a goal of going, not merely the setting of another action. The routine sentence does not assert that you are moving now; the directed sentence does not assert that you have arrived.

depth.definitions: Teaching grammars call these patterns unidirectional and multidirectional, or one-way and non-one-way. Unidirectional presents movement along one direction on a particular occasion. Non-one-way includes several patterns: repeated trips, round trips in appropriate contexts, and movement without one sustained direction. Habit is the use practiced here. Both supplied motion verbs are imperfective. They are not a perfective–imperfective pair, a contrast developed in later lessons. A choice between two imperfective motion patterns is logically separate from presenting an activity versus a bounded event. A technical label helps only when attached to an understood distinction.
depth.mechanism: Cornell illustrates directed versus habitual going and also gives a non-one-way walking-around example.[8] Thus “the second verb always means habit” is too narrow. Context helps select the interpretation. A routine question highlights repeated visits; a live route update highlights a directed journey. Add explicit frequency with Я хожу в библиотеку каждый день (ya ha-ZHOO v beeb-lee-a-TYE-ku KAZH-dy DYEN) — I go to the library every day. The time phrase reinforces the habitual reading but does not replace the verb choice. Travel mode is another independent dimension: these are walking verbs, while ordinary vehicle travel requires another pair. A regular train journey cannot be translated accurately by copying a walking verb merely because English uses go for both. Also, a one-way description concerns the leg currently presented; it does not forbid a return journey later.
depth.secondExample: Return to the familiar Я иду домой (ya ee-DOO da-MOY) — I am going home on foot. It describes directed homeward movement, but home is expressed with a special destination adverb rather than the library's preposition-plus-noun pattern. Do not insert the library preposition automatically. This comparison reveals two decisions: choose the motion pattern, then choose an appropriate destination expression. Replacing library with home may require changing phrase structure rather than substituting a dictionary noun. Keep the full models available while learning their internal relationships. A natural English paraphrase can conceal grammatical distinctions that remain important in Russian.
depth.mistake: The first error uses one directed verb whenever English says go. Diagnose whether the context concerns an immediate route or a repeated pattern. The second calls the routine verb perfective because the trips usually end successfully. Aspect is not a tally of successful arrivals, and both verbs here are imperfective. The third assumes a one-way journey means never returning. The present outward leg can be one directed journey even if you return tonight. These corrections distinguish the event under discussion from the larger schedule into which it fits.
depth.application: Optional practice: write two captions for voice messages, one to a friend following your current journey and another explaining your library routine. Use the supplied models, then explain why the second could be true while you remain at home. Model answer: a routine summarizes repeated visits rather than reporting current movement. Self-review checks journey pattern, walking mode, destination, and absence of an invented arrival claim. For transfer, explain in English what additional knowledge would be required to describe a train commute. Do not generate that vocabulary by modifying the walking forms. Recognizing a knowledge boundary is more accurate than inventing a plausible word.
depth.summary: Motion pattern, travel mode, destination, and completion are separate choices. This lesson supplies a narrow walking contrast, not all motion verbs. Next use a regular past-tense pattern to describe earlier activities while preserving the participant roles from the first unit.

lessons.title: Past agreement follows the subject
lessons.explanation: Your earlier feminine past reading phrase can now become a productive pattern. Compare Я читала книгу (ya chee-TA-la KNEE-gu) — I read / was reading a book; feminine past and Я читал книгу (ya chee-TAL KNEE-gu) — I read / was reading a book; masculine past. The verb changes according to the singular subject's grammatical gender, while the book remains the direct object. The objective is to describe a past activity using the supplied subject pattern without making the verb agree with the object. Keep past agreement and noun case as separate decisions. This is an extension of familiar material, not an instruction to memorize all irregular Russian past forms. A reliable small set of contrasts supports later generalization better than an undifferentiated list.
lessons.example: A speaker using feminine singular agreement reports an earlier reading session with Я читала книгу (ya chee-TA-la KNEE-gu) — I read / was reading a book; feminine past. A speaker using masculine agreement describes the same activity and object with Я читал книгу (ya chee-TAL KNEE-gu) — I read / was reading a book; masculine past. The book remains accusative. A group instead says Мы читали книгу (my chee-TA-lee KNEE-gu) — We read / were reading a book. The plural past form does not divide into feminine and masculine versions in the way singular forms do. Identify the subject first, select its past agreement pattern, and then preserve the noun's direct-object role. Do not change every word because one grammatical feature has changed. These examples isolate agreement by keeping the reading activity and object stable.

depth.definitions: Agreement is the matching of grammatical features between related words. In these past sentences, the verb matches the subject in gender and number, not through separate first-person and third-person endings. Number distinguishes singular from plural. An infinitive is a dictionary-style verb form, such as Читать (chee-TAT) — to read, that does not identify who acts or when. A suffix is a grammatical piece attached to a stem. The familiar regular past pattern combines a past marker with gender or number marking. Those terms describe evidence; they should not encourage mechanically producing unlearned irregular verbs.
depth.mechanism: Cornell explains regular past formation and subject agreement, while noting irregular stems, suffix behavior, and stress.[9] Reading illustrates the straightforward pattern. The first-person pronoun does not itself specify gender, so the singular past verb supplies a distinction absent from that pronoun. Plural agreement behaves differently and does not repeat the singular gender contrast. Grammatical gender should not be treated as an evaluation of a person's ability or social role. Use the forms appropriate to the speaker or reference rather than guessing from stereotypes. Time remains separate from aspect: all three reading models concern the past, yet none specifically asserts that the whole book was finished. A correct past ending cannot answer every question about an event's structure.
depth.secondExample: Now analyze Анна писала ручкой (AN-na pee-SA-la ROOCH-kay) — Anna wrote / was writing with a pen. Anna is the subject and controls feminine singular past agreement. The pen is an implement, so its instrumental form comes from the construction learned earlier. Its grammatical gender does not control the verb. This transfers the agreement principle from reading an object to writing with a tool. If subject and implement happen to share grammatical features, the resemblance is incidental. Locate the controller before matching endings, or you may produce a correct sentence for the wrong reason and fail as soon as the object or implement changes.
depth.mistake: A common error says the reading verb is feminine because the book noun is feminine. Test that account against the masculine speaker example: the book stays the same while the verb changes. Another imports English person agreement and expects different past endings for I and she even when both require feminine singular. That contrast is not required here. A third treats the regular infinitive-to-past recipe as universal. The motion family includes irregular past forms, so do not attach a regular ending to a familiar present motion form and assume the result is valid.
depth.application: Optional practice: make three columns for a feminine speaker, masculine speaker, and group reading. Circle what changes on the verb and mark what stays constant on the object. Model explanation: the subject controls past agreement; the book retains its accusative role. Then label subject, past verb, and implement in Anna's writing sentence. Self-review checks controller, number, learned verb form, and noun role. Explain why keeping an identical object across two sentences is useful evidence about what does not control the verb. Practice the forms you need actively, while retaining recognition of the complete contrast.
depth.summary: Past agreement and noun case operate together but answer different questions. A past activity can be reported without asserting its endpoint. The next lesson keeps the reading context and separates time from the presentation of a completed event.

lessons.title: Activity versus a bounded reading event
lessons.explanation: Past time does not by itself tell a listener whether a whole book was read through. Compare Я читала книгу (ya chee-TA-la KNEE-gu) — I read / was reading a book; feminine, activity-focused and Я прочитала книгу (ya pra-chee-TA-la KNEE-gu) — I read the book through / finished reading the book; feminine. Both are past with feminine singular agreement. The first presents reading as activity or reports its occurrence without specifically asserting completion. The second presents reading the book as a bounded whole. The objective is to select a report that fits the evidence rather than equating every past event with a finished result. This distinction is called aspect. Begin with a concrete contrast, and only then attach the grammatical labels.
lessons.example: A reader spends the evening reading but stops halfway. The activity model Я читала книгу (ya chee-TA-la KNEE-gu) — I read / was reading a book; feminine, activity-focused fits, while the completed-event model would overstate the evidence. On another occasion she reads the entire book and reports readiness to discuss its ending. Use Я прочитала книгу (ya pra-chee-TA-la KNEE-gu) — I read the book through / finished reading the book; feminine to present that bounded result. First identify time: both events are earlier. Next identify viewpoint: activity or a bounded event. Finally retain feminine past agreement and the accusative object. The prefix changes the aspectual choice in this learned pair; it does not make the book change case or the subject become plural.

depth.definitions: Aspect is a grammatical way of presenting event structure and boundaries, distinct from tense, which locates an event in time. Imperfective labels Читать (chee-TAT) — to read; imperfective, and perfective labels Прочитать (pra-chee-TAT) — to read through; perfective. A bounded event is presented as a whole with a relevant limit. For this reading pair and book object, the limit is reading the book through. Perfective does not mean excellent or morally perfect; imperfective does not mean defective. They classify grammatical forms and uses rather than intellectual ability. An aspect partner is a related verb used for a corresponding aspectual presentation, but related verbs may differ in additional lexical meaning.
depth.mechanism: Cornell distinguishes aspect from tense and warns that an endpoint explanation is not a complete selection algorithm.[7] Two limits matter immediately. Imperfective does not assert failure to finish: it can report an activity without foregrounding its endpoint. An event completed in reality can sometimes be described imperfectively when discourse calls for that view. Conversely, not every perfective verb means finishing an entire object. Perfective verbs may package beginnings, single occurrences, or bounded stretches according to their lexical meaning. Learn real pairs and their uses rather than assuming a prefix performs the same operation on every verb. Spanish imperfect and preterite can help you notice viewpoint, but they do not provide a one-to-one translation system for Russian aspect.
depth.secondExample: Suppose a tutor asks what occupied your evening rather than whether an assignment is complete. An activity-focused reply can be relevant even if you happened to reach the final page. If a partner instead asks whether you can discuss the ending, the bounded report gives more relevant information about coverage. The event in the world may be identical, yet the communicative question differs. Grammar organizes what the speaker asserts and what remains implicit. This explains why aspect learning requires attention to conversational purposes as well as a physical timeline of actions.
depth.mistake: The seductive shortcut is “imperfective means unfinished.” Ask whether the sentence denies completion or merely leaves it unasserted. Our activity model does the latter. Another error treats the prefix as an English-style past marker. Both forms are already past through their endings; aspect adds an independent distinction. A third copies the prefix onto any verb whose English meaning seems finishable. That generates unreliable vocabulary. Keep the supplied pair together and consult a dictionary or an authoritative model when extending your inventory.
depth.application: Optional practice: make scenario A stop before the book's end and scenario B explicitly finish it for discussion. Match the supplied sentences to the intended reports. Model answer: A supports the activity report; B supports a bounded-event report foregrounding completion. Self-review checks time, subject agreement, object case, and whether the endpoint claim exceeds the evidence. Finally explain why a completed real-world reading does not make every imperfective description false. That explanation distinguishes a missing assertion from a denial and prevents an initially useful simplification from becoming a persistent misunderstanding.
depth.summary: Aspect concerns how an event is presented, not merely when it occurs. This pair makes a book-reading endpoint explicit without changing participant roles. The next lesson uses the distinction to form two different kinds of future statement.

lessons.question: Does imperfective past reading necessarily deny completion?

lessons.distractor: Yes; it always says completion was impossible.
lessons.correction: Leaving an endpoint unasserted is not denying that it happened.

lessons.title: Future activity and future result
lessons.explanation: Your earlier future reading phrase described activity without specifying an entire book's completion. Compare Я буду читать книгу (ya BOO-du chee-TAT KNEE-gu) — I will read / be reading a book with Я прочитаю книгу (ya pra-chee-TA-yu KNEE-gu) — I will read the book through. The first combines a future auxiliary with an imperfective infinitive. The second uses a perfective verb with personal endings and projects a bounded event. The objective is to select a future construction matching the content of a plan. Allocating an afternoon to reading need not promise a completed book. A plan to read the book through includes the endpoint in what is projected, but grammatical form cannot guarantee that reality will fulfill a prediction or promise.
lessons.example: You reserve tomorrow afternoon for reading and do not know how far you will get. Choose Я буду читать книгу (ya BOO-du chee-TAT KNEE-gu) — I will read / be reading a book. The auxiliary places the activity in the future; the infinitive identifies reading. If you instead undertake to read the assigned book through before discussion, use Я прочитаю книгу (ya pra-chee-TA-yu KNEE-gu) — I will read the book through without adding another future auxiliary. Compare present Я читаю книгу (ya chee-TA-yu KNEE-gu) — I am reading a book / I read a book with the perfective future. Their personal endings can look related, but aspect changes their basic time interpretation. Identify aspect before automatically calling a personal form present tense. English will does not reveal the full structure of either Russian option.

depth.definitions: An auxiliary is a helping verb contributing grammatical information to another verb. An infinitive does not agree with the actor. In the compound future, the auxiliary carries the personal form while the imperfective infinitive stays unchanged. Non-past endings are personal endings whose basic time interpretation depends on aspect: imperfective normally expresses present in these models, while perfective expresses future. A projected endpoint belongs to the content of a prediction, intention, or promise. It is not evidence that the event has occurred, nor a measure of how trustworthy the speaker is.
depth.mechanism: Cornell lays out both future patterns and contrasts them with present and past forms.[10] This explains why an English-style future helper cannot simply be added to every Russian infinitive. It also explains why the perfective personal form is not an ordinary ongoing-present report. Special discourse uses exist beyond this basic chart; our goal is accurate ordinary literal production, not an exhaustive theory of tense. Add an explicit day with Завтра я буду читать (ZAF-tra ya BOO-du chee-TAT) — Tomorrow I will read / be reading. Tomorrow clarifies the temporal reference, while the verb construction presents future activity. A time adverb does not rescue an incorrectly assembled verb phrase. Keep the aspect choice and the future formation linked instead of treating them as unrelated memorization tasks.
depth.secondExample: Compare two study agreements. One learner will devote an evening to reading; another will read the book through. If discussion requires the ending, the second agreement addresses that requirement more directly. If the goal is a daily practice habit, the first may be more appropriate. Neither sentence alone establishes future success or states the book's length. The contrast concerns the intended event, not numerical probability. Translating the perfective as guaranteed completion would inflate the speaker's claim beyond what grammar itself warrants. A sincere plan may fail for reasons unrelated to its grammatical form.
depth.mistake: One error interprets the perfective personal form as present because it resembles a familiar present ending. Check aspect first. Another combines the future auxiliary with the perfective infinitive by borrowing pieces from both models. Keep these ordinary constructions separate. A third selects a result-oriented future merely to sound confident when the intended commitment is only to spend time reading. That is not simply a stylistic improvement: it changes what is promised. Choose the activity model when you intend to leave the endpoint open.
depth.application: Optional practice: write a calendar note reserving reading time and a separate commitment to finish the book for discussion. Match them to the supplied future models. Model explanation: the calendar note foregrounds activity and uses the compound imperfective future; the endpoint commitment uses the perfective future. Self-review checks aspect, verb construction, object form, and the scope of the promise. Then compare the present reading model with the perfective future and identify why their similar personal endings do not imply the same time. Explain in English first if that helps separate conceptual understanding from pronunciation retrieval.
depth.summary: Future reference has more than one grammatical route. Distinguish planned activity from a projected bounded event, and distinguish both from evidence of actual completion. The final lesson coordinates roles, movement, time, and aspect in a connected account.

lessons.title: Connect events without inventing results
lessons.explanation: A connected account helps listeners recover who did what, where, and when without converting assumptions into asserted facts. The objective is to coordinate this level's constructions in a short sequence and explain the choices. Use three time anchors: yesterday, now, and tomorrow. Each sentence can remain simple. Connection does not require advanced subordinate clauses or new vocabulary added merely for decoration. Depth lies in coordinating event roles, temporal reference, motion pattern, and aspect accurately. A dependable short account is more useful than an elaborate paragraph whose grammar obscures what actually happened.
lessons.example: Consider a modeled account from a speaker using feminine past agreement: Вчера я читала книгу в библиотеке (fchee-RA ya chee-TA-la KNEE-gu v beeb-lee-a-TYE-kye) — Yesterday I read / was reading a book in the library; feminine. Next, Сейчас я иду домой с Анной (see-CHAS ya ee-DOO da-MOY s AN-nay) — Now I am going home on foot with Anna. Finally, Завтра я прочитаю книгу (ZAF-tra ya pra-chee-TA-yu KNEE-gu) — Tomorrow I will read the book through. The first identifies past reading, its object, and its setting. The second updates a current directed journey and names a companion. The third projects a bounded future reading event. Analyze each sentence before speaking the sequence smoothly. Yesterday's activity does not specifically assert a completed book, so tomorrow's plan need not contradict it. The account also leaves today's starting point and Anna's activities yesterday unstated. Avoid adding them to the translation.

depth.definitions: A time anchor places an event relative to the moment of speaking or another reference point. Cohesion connects parts of a text: recurring participants, the book, and a temporal sequence help here. An assertion is what a speaker commits to saying; an inference is a conclusion a listener draws using context. A rubric is an explicit set of criteria for evaluating work. Our rubric separates communicative accuracy, grammatical form, and pronunciation intelligibility, so a difficulty in one dimension does not erase success in another. These distinctions make feedback more precise than a single impression of fluency.
depth.mechanism: The source tense chart distinguishes past, imperfective future activity, and perfective future event.[10] The aspect explanation cautions against reducing imperfective to noncompletion.[7] Apply both to the account. Yesterday's reading does not assert the final page was reached; tomorrow's perfective projects reading through. The repeated book creates continuity, but rereading remains possible, so do not infer that every future page must be new. In the current sentence, the walking verb presents one directed leg, the homeward adverb supplies the goal, and the accompaniment phrase supplies Anna's role. Each clause selects its own construction. A library location in one sentence does not force the next sentence to use a library-style noun phrase for home.
depth.secondExample: Change one fact: tomorrow contains only a limited reading period and no promise to read through. Substitute Завтра я буду читать книгу (ZAF-tra ya BOO-du chee-TAT KNEE-gu) — Tomorrow I will read / be reading a book for the final sentence and leave the earlier sentences unchanged. This controlled revision isolates the aspectual commitment while retaining time, subject, and object. Now change a different fact in English: Anna receives a written message rather than walks alongside the speaker. The accompaniment model cannot express that relation; choose the earlier writing-to-Anna construction. Some revisions require a different verb pattern, not merely one new noun ending. Track which part of meaning changes before editing the form.
depth.mistake: A common error allows one grammatical choice to spread across the sequence: yesterday's feminine past ending does not belong on tomorrow's personal future form. Another translates past activity as finished yesterday or directed walking as arrived now, inventing endpoints. A third treats recognizing the models as proof of independent production. Cover the model and attempt an account, then compare. If analysis is correct but retrieval slow, practice recall. If an unsupported inference persists, revisit the conceptual contrast instead of merely repeating the paragraph faster. Different errors deserve different practice.
depth.application: Optional level project: produce the three-sentence fictional account and revise its future when the plan changes. Model commentary: past agreement follows the speaker; book is accusative; library is a setting; the current walk is directed motion with a companion; future aspect distinguishes activity allocation from a projected result. Rubric: match the scenario, preserve participant roles, choose appropriate time and aspect, retain intelligible marked stress, and avoid unsupported English inferences. Mark each criterion secure, developing, or needs review, citing a sentence as evidence. No score from this small task certifies unrestricted fluency. Keep reading completion distinct from demonstrated production.
depth.summary: You have authored a bounded account, not mastered Russian grammar. Use the unit quiz and longer level assessment to locate gaps. Review case roles for participant confusion, motion patterns for routine-versus-route errors, and aspect for endpoint overclaims. Return later to the same task with the models covered to test durable retrieval.

questions.distractor: Verb and book must receive the same feminine ending.

questions.distractor: Every library mention must retain one identical case form.

questions.distractor: The future plan proves you already possess the book.

questions.distractor: I am on a directed homeward walk with Anna as companion.
questions.correction: Directed motion does not establish arrival.

questions.prompt: A book was read through, but the question asks what occupied the evening. Must an imperfective report be false?
questions.answer: No: activity presentation can leave a real endpoint unasserted.
questions.distractor: Yes: imperfective always denies completion in reality.
questions.correction: Aspect organizes the assertion; an omitted endpoint is not a denial.

questions.distractor: Perfective future as a guarantee with a nominative book object.

lessons.title: Adjectives copy their noun
lessons.explanation: Russian adjectives change shape to match the noun they describe. They agree in gender, number, and case. English keeps one word forever: a new table, a new book, new shoes, a new idea. Russian does not. It says новый стол (NO-vyj stol, a new table) for a masculine noun, новая книга (NO-va-ya KNEE-ga, a new book) for a feminine one, новое окно (NO-va-ye ak-NO, a new window) for a neuter one, and новые дома (NO-vy-ye da-MA, new houses) for a plural. The ending is not decoration. It repeats information about the noun, so your listener hears the gender twice: once from the adjective and once from the noun. That redundancy is a gift. It keeps meaning intact when word order shifts, when a word is swallowed, or when someone speaks quickly past a word you missed. The dictionary form of an adjective ends in -ый or -ий, and that is the masculine form. Feminine changes it to -ая or -яя, neuter to -ое or -ее, and plural to -ые or -ие. The choice between the hard and soft versions follows the final consonant of the stem, not the meaning. Learn the four endings as one single pattern with four positions, never as four unrelated facts to memorize.
lessons.example: Imagine you are describing a room to a friend. You see a table, a lamp, and two chairs. A Russian speaker says: это новый стол (EH-ta NO-vyj stol, this is a new table), это новая лампа (EH-ta NO-va-ya LAM-pa, this is a new lamp), and это новые стулья (EH-ta NO-vy-ye STOOL-ya, these are new chairs). Notice that the adjective changed three times while the meaning new never changed at all. The noun told the adjective what to do. You are not choosing an ending for your own convenience. You are obeying the noun you already said.
lessons.question: A learner wants to say a new book and writes новый книга. What has gone wrong, and what rule repairs it?
lessons.answer: The adjective kept its masculine dictionary ending while describing a feminine noun. The repair is to match the adjective to the noun: книга is feminine, so the adjective takes the feminine ending -ая and the phrase becomes новая книга.
lessons.distractor: The noun книга should be changed into a masculine noun so that новый agrees with it.
lessons.correction: You cannot change a noun's gender to suit an adjective; gender belongs to the noun. The adjective is the follower, so the adjective changes. книга is feminine by its ending and by usage, so the adjective becomes новая. This is why the reliable habit is to learn a noun together with its gender from the first day.

depth.definitions: Agreement is the requirement that a modifier carry the same gender, number, and case as the noun it modifies. The dictionary form of an adjective is its masculine nominative singular. A stem is the part of the word that carries meaning, before the ending is attached.
depth.mechanism: A Russian adjective carries an ending that encodes three things at once: gender, number, and case. When you build a phrase, the noun is the authority. The noun's ending announces its own gender, number, and case, and the adjective must broadcast the same values. Masculine nouns usually end in a consonant, feminine in -а or -я, neuter in -о or -е. Because the adjective copies the noun rather than leading it, the practical order of thought is: decide the noun and its role, then dress the adjective to match. This is why Russian tolerates flexible word order. Since agreement carries the grammatical information, moving words around does not destroy the sentence's meaning.
depth.secondExample: Compare a description of two different objects where only the noun changes: я вижу большой дом (ya VEE-zhoo bal-SHOJ dom, I see a big house) and я вижу большую книгу (ya VEE-zhoo bal-SHOO-yoo KNEE-goo, I see a big book). The adjective shifted twice: once for gender, once for case, because книга in this sentence is the direct object. The noun drove both changes.
depth.mistake: The commonest beginner error is freezing the adjective in its dictionary shape because that is the form in the word list. A second frequent error is matching the adjective to the gender of an English translation rather than the Russian noun; translation gender is irrelevant. A third is applying an ending by sound alone without checking the noun's case, which produces phrases that sound plausible but mark the wrong role.
depth.application: Choose five objects in the room around you. For each one, write a Russian phrase with an adjective plus noun, then say aloud which gender and number you matched and why. Model response for a window: новое окно (NO-va-ye ak-NO) uses the neuter ending -ое because окно is a neuter noun ending in -о. Then take the same five adjectives and deliberately attach each to a noun of a different gender, and note how many endings you had to change.
depth.summary: Russian adjectives agree with their noun in gender, number, and case. The noun is the authority and the adjective follows. Learn four endings as one pattern, and always learn a new noun with its gender attached.

lessons.title: Asking which one: какой
lessons.explanation: The question word какой (ka-KOJ, which, what kind) behaves exactly like an adjective, so it also changes to match the noun it asks about. Masculine: какой. Feminine: какая. Neuter: какое. Plural: какие. This is convenient, because you already learned the adjective pattern in the previous lesson and can transfer it whole. Use какой when you are asking about a quality or an identity among options: какой фильм? (ka-KOJ feelm, which film?) asks the listener to select or describe. Compare this with кто (kto, who) for people as persons and что (shto, what) for things as things. The difference matters in conversation. If you ask что это? (SHTO EH-ta, what is this?) you are asking for a category or identity. If you ask какой это фильм? you are asking what kind of film it is, and the answer will be a description: good, long, old, French. Notice that как (kak, how) is a different word and asks about manner or degree, while какой asks about a characteristic attached to a noun. When the answer comes, it will arrive in the same shape as the question, which is how you can confirm you asked correctly.
lessons.example: You are at a market looking at two bags. You point and ask: какая сумка лучше? (ka-KA-ya SOOM-ka LOOT-she, which bag is better?) The question word какая is feminine because сумка is feminine. The seller answers: эта сумка лучше (EH-ta SOOM-ka LOOT-she, this bag is better). Now you look at two phones. The same question becomes какой телефон лучше? (ka-KOJ tee-lee-FON LOOT-she, which phone is better?) Only the question word changed. The strategy did not.
lessons.question: Why does какой change its ending while кто and что do not?
lessons.answer: Какой behaves as an adjective attached to a noun, so it must agree with that noun in gender and number. Кто and что are pronouns standing in for the whole person or thing, so they have no noun to agree with and keep one form.
lessons.distractor: Какой changes because it is a longer word, and longer Russian words always carry more endings.
lessons.correction: Length has nothing to do with it. Grammatical role decides which words inflect. Какой modifies a noun and therefore agrees with it, exactly like an adjective. Кто and что replace a noun outright, so there is no noun whose features they must copy. Compare: какая книга (which book) but кто это (who is this).

depth.definitions: A modifier is a word that adds information to a noun. Agreement is copying the noun's gender, number, and case. Interrogative words ask questions; some are modifiers and some are standalone pronouns.
depth.mechanism: Какой works as a modifier, so it inherits the agreement requirement. Its four forms map onto the four adjective positions you already know: -ой for masculine, -ая for feminine, -ое for neuter, -ие for plural. Because the ending is predictable, the practical skill is not memorizing four words but recognizing that your question word must match whatever noun you are asking about. This also gives you a fast self-check: if your question word disagrees with your noun, you will hear it as wrong before you can explain why. A second self-check is positional. Because какой normally stands immediately before the noun it describes, an ending that disagrees with the very next word is easy to notice while you are still speaking, which means you can correct yourself mid-sentence rather than after the fact.
depth.secondExample: Ask about a person's character rather than an object: какой он человек? (ka-KOJ on chee-la-VYEK, what kind of person is he?) Here человек is masculine, so какой stays masculine. Now ask about a group: какие они люди? (ka-KEE-ye a-NEE LOO-dee, what kind of people are they?) The plural noun люди pulls the question word into its plural form.
depth.mistake: A frequent error is using что when asking for a description, which produces a question about category where a question about quality was intended. Another is leaving какой in its masculine form while asking about a feminine noun, which sounds as jarring to a Russian speaker as the wrong article in Spanish. A third is confusing как with какой; как asks how something is done, какой asks what kind it is.
depth.application: Write five questions about objects within reach, each using какой in the correct form for its noun. Then answer each one yourself in a full phrase. Model: какая чашка тебе нравится? (ka-KA-ya CHASH-ka tee-BYE NRA-veet-sya, which cup do you like?) followed by мне нравится эта чашка (mnye NRA-veet-sya EH-ta CHASH-ka, I like this cup).
depth.summary: Какой is a question adjective and agrees with the noun you ask about. Use какой for qualities, кто for persons, что for categories, and как for manner.

lessons.title: Comparing two things
lessons.explanation: To compare two things in Russian you can use a short comparative form that behaves like an adjective, or a longer phrase built with более. The short form is the one you will hear most often. Most adjectives form it by dropping the ending and adding -ее: красивый becomes красивее (kra-SEE-vee-ye, more beautiful), интересный becomes интереснее (in-tee-RYES-nee-ye, more interesting). A handful of very common adjectives form the comparative irregularly and you should simply learn them: хороший becomes лучше (LOOT-she, better), плохой becomes хуже (KHOO-zhe, worse), большой becomes больше (BOL-she, bigger), маленький becomes меньше (MYEN-she, smaller). The longer option with более plus the unchanged dictionary adjective is the safe fallback when you do not know the short form; it is fully correct and simply sounds more formal. Once the comparative is in hand, the word for than is чем (chem), and the thing being compared against goes into a form that marks it, often with чем or with the genitive. In speech you will frequently hear the genitive without чем: эта книга интереснее той (EH-ta KNEE-ga in-tee-RYES-nee-ye toj, this book is more interesting than that one).
lessons.example: You are choosing between two routes to work. A colleague says: этот путь короче (EH-tat poot KO-ro-che, this route is shorter) and adds: но та дорога удобнее (no ta da-RO-ga oo-DOB-nee-ye, but that road is more convenient). Two different adjectives, one comparison each, no extra words required. If you then want to name what you are comparing against, you say эта дорога удобнее, чем та (EH-ta da-RO-ga oo-DOB-nee-ye chem ta, this road is more convenient than that one).
lessons.question: A learner says эта книга более интереснее. Why is this phrase wrong even though both parts are real Russian words?
lessons.answer: The phrase marks the comparison twice. Более already means more, and the ending -ее also marks the comparative, so the two devices conflict. Use one: эта книга более интересная or эта книга интереснее.
lessons.distractor: The phrase is wrong because более may only be used with verbs rather than with adjectives.
lessons.correction: Более combines freely with adjectives; that is its whole purpose. The error is double marking, not the choice of word. In Russian, as in most careful writing, one comparison signal per comparison. Choose the short comparative if you want a conversational tone, or более plus the full adjective if you want a formal one, but never both at once.

depth.definitions: A comparative expresses that one thing has more of a quality than another. The positive form is the plain adjective with no comparison attached. An irregular comparative is one that does not follow the regular ending pattern and must be memorized as a whole word.
depth.mechanism: The regular comparative is formed by removing the adjective's ending and attaching -ее to the stem. Because the resulting word is a comparison rather than a description of a noun's gender, the short comparative does not change for gender or number. This is a genuine simplification and worth noticing: лучше works for a masculine noun, a feminine noun, and a plural alike. The more formal analytical comparative leaves the adjective untouched and puts более in front, which is why it never creates agreement problems either. One practical consequence deserves stating plainly. Because the short comparative does not inflect, you never need to check its gender before speaking, and the only remaining decision is whether the comparison requires a second item to be named. Learners who expect an ending where none is needed often invent one, which is a common source of the errors described below.
depth.secondExample: Compare people rather than objects. Он старше меня (on STAr-she mee-NYA, he is older than me) uses the irregular comparative старше and the genitive form меня. Then widen the comparison: она самая старшая в семье (a-NA SA-ma-ya STAr-sha-ya v seem-YE, she is the oldest in the family), which shifts from comparing two to ranking within a group.
depth.mistake: The most common error is double marking with более plus the -ее ending. A second is attaching a gender ending to a short comparative, producing forms like лучшая in a context where the comparison has no noun to agree with. A third is forgetting that a few high frequency adjectives are irregular and inventing a regular form such as хорошее instead of using лучше.
depth.application: Write six comparisons about your own day: two objects, two places, two activities. Use at least one irregular comparative and at least one чем construction. Model: метро быстрее автобуса (meet-RO BYST-ree-ye af-TO-boo-sa, the metro is faster than the bus), then say the same idea formally with более.
depth.summary: Regular comparatives end in -ее; a small set are irregular and must be memorized whole. Mark the comparison once, never twice, and use чем or the genitive to name what you are comparing against.

lessons.title: The most: самый and всех
lessons.explanation: Russian expresses the highest degree in two main ways. The first is самый (SA-myj, most) placed before the adjective, forming a phrase that behaves like an ordinary adjective and therefore agrees with the noun: самый интересный фильм (SA-myj in-tee-RYES-nyj feelm, the most interesting film), самая интересная книга (SA-ma-ya in-tee-RYES-na-ya KNEE-ga, the most interesting book). Because самый is a modifier, it carries the same gender and number endings you learned for adjectives. The second way uses the comparative followed by всех (vsekh, of all) or всего (vsye-VO, of everything): она читает быстрее всех (a-NA chee-TA-yeet BYST-ree-ye vsekh, she reads faster than everyone). Notice how the two strategies divide labour. Самый ranks a noun by attaching to a plain adjective, while всех attaches to a comparative and ranks a person or thing against a whole set. Do not mix them: the phrase самый быстрее combines a ranking word with a comparative and is not standard. A useful instinct is that самый answers the question which one, while всех answers the question compared to whom or what.
lessons.example: You are describing your week. Today was the hardest day: сегодня был самый трудный день (see-VOD-nya byl SA-myj TROOD-nyj dyehn). Then you want to say that today you worked more than on any other day: сегодня я работал больше всех (see-VOD-nya ya ra-BO-tal BOL-she vsekh). The first sentence ranks the day itself, so самый attaches to the adjective and agrees with день. The second sentence ranks your effort against everyone else, so больше takes всех.
lessons.question: Why is самый больше всех not an acceptable way to say the most of all?
lessons.answer: It stacks two different ranking systems on one word. Самый attaches to a plain adjective to rank a noun, and больше is already a comparative. Choose one structure: самый большой for the largest, or больше всех for larger than all others.
lessons.distractor: It is unacceptable because больше is informal and самый may only be followed by adjectives borrowed from other languages.
lessons.correction: Formality has nothing to do with it, and самый combines with ordinary native adjectives constantly. The problem is structural. A superlative phrase needs either самый plus a plain adjective or a comparative plus всех. Combining them marks the comparison twice, just as более plus интереснее does in the previous lesson.

depth.definitions: The superlative ranks one member of a set above all others. A plain or positive adjective carries no comparison. A comparative measures two or more items against each other without claiming a top rank.
depth.mechanism: Самый is an adjective-like modifier, so it agrees with the noun in gender, number, and case, and the adjective after it stays plain. The всех construction works differently: it takes a comparative, which already carries the comparison, and adds a word meaning of all to supply the set. That is why the two cannot be merged. The choice is driven by what you are ranking. Ranking a noun calls for самый. Ranking an action or a person's performance relative to a group calls for the comparative plus всех. One further detail keeps the two structures from blurring. Самый must agree with the noun, so the noun's gender is checked before the superlative is spoken, while a comparative plus всех carries no agreement at all because the comparative does not inflect. That asymmetry is a useful test. If you find yourself choosing an ending for the ranking word, you are building the самый structure; if there is no ending to choose, you are building the comparative structure. Noticing which decision you are making prevents the two from being combined by accident.
depth.secondExample: Compare ranking within a family: это самый старший сын (EH-ta SA-myj STAr-sheej syn, this is the eldest son) ranks the son among the sons by attaching самый to a plain adjective. Now rank behaviour: он помогает больше всех (on pa-ma-GA-yeet BOL-she vsekh, he helps more than anyone) uses the comparative plus всех because the thing being ranked is an action.
depth.mistake: Learners often produce самый plus a comparative. Another common slip is failing to make самый agree, writing самый книга instead of самая книга. A third is using всех when comparing only two items, where an ordinary comparative is enough. A final slip is forgetting that самый already carries the meaning of most, so adding very for extra emphasis produces a phrase that argues with itself.
depth.application: Write four superlative statements about your own life: your most useful book, your most difficult day, your fastest route, and who in a group helps most. Use самый twice and a comparative plus всех twice, then explain in one line why each structure was the right choice.
depth.summary: Use самый plus a plain agreeing adjective to rank a noun, and a comparative plus всех to rank an action or person against a group. Never combine the two.
