lessons.title: Quantity: сколько, много, and counting
lessons.explanation: Quantity in Russian is bound up with the genitive case, and the pattern rewards attention once. The question word сколько (SKOL-ka, how much, how many) is followed by the genitive plural for countable things and the genitive singular for mass nouns: сколько книг (SKOL-ka kneek, how many books), сколько времени (SKOL-ka VRYE-mee-nee, how much time). The words много (MNO-ga, much, many) and мало (MA-la, little, few) behave the same way and are also followed by the genitive. The truly important pattern is the agreement of numbers one through four. After один the noun is singular nominative. After два, три, and четыре the noun is genitive singular: два стола (dva sta-LA, two tables), три книги (tree KNEE-gee, three books). From пять upward the noun takes the genitive plural: пять столов (pyat sta-LOV, five tables), десять книг (DYE-seet kneek, ten books). The logic is not arbitrary. The lower numbers historically behaved like modifiers, so they kept a shape closer to the noun's own form, while higher numbers behaved like nouns of quantity, which in Russian govern the genitive.
lessons.example: You are shopping. You say: мне нужно два килограмма яблок (mnye NOOZH-na dva kee-la-GRA-ma YA-blak, I need two kilograms of apples). The number два is followed by a genitive singular килограмма, and the thing being measured is in the genitive plural яблок. Then you adjust: лучше три килограмма (LOOT-she tree kee-la-GRA-ma, better three kilograms). Three also takes the genitive singular. If you need more, the shape changes: пять килограммов (pyat kee-la-GRAM-maf, five kilograms) takes the genitive plural.
lessons.question: Why does the noun change after пять but not after три?
lessons.answer: Numbers from two to four are followed by the genitive singular, while numbers from five upward are followed by the genitive plural. Три килограмма uses the singular; пять килограммов uses the plural.
lessons.distractor: Because пять is a longer word than три, and Russian shortens the noun after longer numbers to keep speech balanced.
lessons.correction: Word length does not affect grammar here. The difference follows the historical behaviour of the numerals. Two, three, and four patterned with the noun and kept a singular form, while five and above patterned as nouns of quantity, which in Russian require the genitive. That is why the split falls exactly between four and five instead of anywhere else.

depth.definitions: The genitive is the case used for possession, absence, and quantity. A mass noun names something not counted in units, such as water or time. A countable noun names things you can count one by one.
depth.mechanism: Quantity words such as сколько, много, and мало require the genitive because they express an unspecified amount rather than a specific count. The numerals then override the default with their own pattern. The result is a three part rule. One takes the singular nominative. Two through four take the genitive singular. Five and above take the genitive plural. Once you internalize the boundary between four and five, most quantity sentences become predictable rather than memorized. Two extensions follow from the same logic and are worth adding once the base rule is secure. Mass nouns such as time and water do not take a plural in this pattern, so you say much time rather than a count with a plural noun. And compound numerals above twenty follow the ending of their final element, so twenty-one behaves like one and twenty-two behaves like two, which means the boundary rule applies to the last word of the number rather than to the size of the number.
depth.secondExample: Apply the same rule to people: один студент (a-DEEN stoo-DYENT, one student), два студента (dva stoo-DYEN-ta, two students), пять студентов (pyat stoo-DYEN-taf, five students). The noun moved from nominative singular to genitive singular to genitive plural while the meaning changed only in number. Notice that the noun carries the only change; the numbers themselves stayed fixed while the noun moved through its forms.
depth.mistake: The most common error is using the nominative plural after two, three, or four, producing shapes like два столы. A second is forgetting that сколько and много also require the genitive rather than the nominative. A third is applying the singular rule to mass nouns, where the genitive singular is the correct default rather than an exception.
depth.application: Write a short shopping list using one, two, three, five, and ten of various items, with the correct noun form after each numeral. Model: один лимон, два лимона, три лимона, пять лимонов. Then ask the price of three of them using сколько.
depth.summary: Quantity words take the genitive. Numerals one, two to four, and five and above each trigger their own noun form, with the key boundary falling between four and five.

questions.answer: It should be новая лампа, because лампа is feminine and the adjective must agree with the noun it modifies.
questions.distractor: It should be новый лампа, because the adjective keeps its dictionary form unless the noun is plural.
questions.correction: Adjectives do not stay in the dictionary form. They copy the gender, number, and case of their noun. Since лампа is feminine, the feminine ending -ая is required.

questions.answer: Какая сумка, because сумка is feminine and какой agrees with the noun it asks about.
questions.distractor: Какой сумка, because какой is the dictionary form and is always acceptable as the default.
questions.correction: Какой is a question adjective and inflects like any other adjective. It must match the gender and number of the noun, so a feminine noun calls for какая.

questions.prompt: A learner writes эта книга более интереснее. Diagnose the error and give two correct alternatives.
questions.answer: The comparison is marked twice. Correct versions are эта книга более интересная and эта книга интереснее.
questions.distractor: Более may only precede verbs, so the adjective should be replaced by a verb form.
questions.correction: Более combines with adjectives, but it must not be paired with the short comparative ending -ее. Choose one strategy: более plus the full adjective, or the short comparative on its own.

questions.prompt: Explain why самый больше всех is not standard Russian and give a correct structure for ranking within a group.
questions.answer: It combines the самый construction with a comparative, marking the ranking twice. A correct form is больше всех, or самый большой if a noun is being ranked.
questions.distractor: It is not standard because самый cannot be used with masculine adjectives at all.
questions.correction: Самый combines with plain adjectives and agrees with the noun. Comparative plus всех ranks an action or a person against a group. The two structures are alternatives, not partners.

questions.prompt: You need to say five tables and two tables. Write both phrases and explain the difference in the noun form.
questions.answer: Пять столов uses the genitive plural because five and above take that form. Два стола uses the genitive singular because two through four do.
questions.distractor: Both take the nominative plural, because any number above one makes the noun plural.
questions.correction: Russian divides the numerals at the boundary between four and five. Two, three, and four take the genitive singular, while five and above take the genitive plural.

lessons.title: Joining ideas: и, а, но
lessons.explanation: Three short conjunctions carry most of the connecting work in spoken Russian, and their differences matter more than their length suggests. И (ee, and) simply adds information without implying any contrast: я читаю и пишу (ya chee-TA-yoo ee pee-SHOO, I read and write). А (a, and, but, while) signals a shift or a mild contrast between two things set side by side, and it is the connector learners most often get wrong. Compare я студент, а он врач (ya stoo-DYENT a on vrach, I am a student and he is a doctor). Nothing here is a strong objection. The speaker is contrasting two different roles. НО (no, but) marks a genuine contrast or a limitation: я хочу поехать, но нет времени (ya ha-CHOO pa-YE-khat no nyet VRYE-mee-nee, I want to go but there is no time). The practical difference is degree. И says here is more. А says here is something different, side by side. НО says here is something that pushes against what I just said. Russian also tolerates starting a sentence with а, which English does not do with and, so you will hear а at the beginning of replies as a gentle pivot: а ты? (a ty, and you?).
lessons.example: You are telling a colleague about your weekend. You say: я работал и учился (ya ra-BO-tal ee oo-CHEEL-sya, I worked and studied), which simply lists two activities. Then you add contrast about a friend: а он отдыхал (a on at-dy-KHAL, while he rested). The а signals the pivot from your weekend to his, not a complaint. Finally you add the limitation: я хотел больше, но не успел (ya ha-TYEL BOL-she no nye oos-PYEL, I wanted more but did not manage it). Three connectors, three different jobs.
lessons.question: A learner wants to say I am tired but happy. Should the connector be и, а, or но, and why?
lessons.answer: Но, because the two qualities pull in different directions and the sentence marks a contrast. The phrase is я устал, но счастлив.
lessons.distractor: И, because both words describe the same person and Russian always joins qualities of one subject with и.
lessons.correction: И joins items without contrast, so it would present tired and happy as a simple list, which loses the speaker's point. А sets two things side by side as different, which is closer but still softer than needed. Но signals a genuine tension between the two states, and that is exactly what the sentence means.

depth.definitions: A conjunction joins words, phrases, or clauses. A coordinating conjunction joins items of equal grammatical weight. A contrast is a relationship in which one statement limits or opposes another.
depth.mechanism: The three conjunctions divide the work of connection by the relationship they encode. И encodes addition with no tension. А encodes juxtaposition, meaning two items are placed next to each other as different or as belonging to different subjects. НО encodes an obstacle or reversal. Because these are relationships rather than fixed translations, the same English and can map onto и or а depending on the relationship. That is why translating word by word produces unnatural Russian, and why paying attention to the relationship first produces the right choice almost automatically.
depth.secondExample: Test the difference with one pair of clauses. Я люблю кофе и чай (I like coffee and tea) lists two drinks I both like. Я люблю кофе, а он чай (I like coffee, while he likes tea) splits the preference between two people. Я люблю кофе, но не пью вечером (I like coffee but do not drink it in the evening) adds a limitation on my own behaviour.
depth.mistake: The most frequent error is using и everywhere, which flattens every relationship into a list and makes speech sound mechanical. A second is using а where a real objection is meant, which understates the speaker's meaning. A third is avoiding sentence-initial а because English forbids sentence-initial and; Russian permits it and uses it constantly in conversation.
depth.application: Take six pairs of statements about your own life and join each pair with the connector that matches its relationship. Label each choice as addition, juxtaposition, or contrast, then read the six sentences aloud. Model: я люблю утро, а вечер трудный (I like the morning, while the evening is hard), labelled as juxtaposition.
depth.summary: И adds, а places two things side by side as different, and но marks real contrast. Choose by relationship, not by matching an English word.

lessons.title: Cause and result: потому что and поэтому
lessons.explanation: Russian marks cause and result with two different words, and keeping them apart prevents a very common confusion. Потому что (pa-ta-MOO shta, because) introduces the reason: я не пришёл, потому что заболел (ya nye pree-SHYOL pa-ta-MOO shta za-ba-LYEL, I did not come because I got ill). The reason follows the connector. Поэтому (pa-EH-ta-moo, therefore, that is why) introduces the result: я заболел, поэтому не пришёл (ya za-ba-LYEL pa-EH-ta-moo nye pree-SHYOL, I got ill, therefore I did not come). The result follows the connector. The two sentences describe the same event, but they start from opposite ends. Notice the internal shape of the words. Потому что contains потому, which relates to that, plus что, the word that joins clauses. Поэтому contains этому, which relates to this, so it points forward to a consequence rather than backward to a cause. Russian word order is flexible, but the relationship between the two clauses is fixed by which connector you chose, so the connector is doing real information work. In speech, потому что is often compressed into a fast stream that sounds like one word, which is why beginners often fail to hear it at first.
lessons.example: You arrive late and explain. Two ways, same facts. Я опоздал, потому что автобус не пришёл (ya a-pa-ZDAL pa-ta-MOO shta af-TO-boos nye pree-SHYOL, I was late because the bus did not come). Or, starting from the cause: автобус не пришёл, поэтому я опоздал (af-TO-boos nye pree-SHYOL pa-EH-ta-moo ya a-pa-ZDAL, the bus did not come, therefore I was late). Choose the order that puts the new information last, since Russian, like English, tends to place the most important point at the end.
lessons.question: A learner writes я устал, потому что не спал. Another writes не спал, поэтому устал. Are both correct, and what is the difference?
lessons.answer: Both are correct. The first states the result and then its cause. The second states the cause and then its result. The connector follows the relationship, not the speaker's preference.
lessons.distractor: Only the first is correct, because потому что must always follow the main statement.
lessons.correction: Neither connector is tied to a fixed position. Потому что introduces a clause expressing the reason, and поэтому introduces a clause expressing the consequence. You can begin with either the cause or the result as long as the connector in the second clause matches the relationship between the two.

depth.definitions: A cause is the reason something happened. A result is what follows from a cause. A subordinate clause is a clause that cannot stand alone and depends on the main clause.
depth.mechanism: Потому что creates a subordinate clause, which is why the clause after it cannot be moved freely to the front of the sentence. Поэтому behaves more like a linking adverb and introduces a main clause, so the sentence that follows can stand on its own. That structural difference explains two practical facts. First, потому что always keeps its place inside the sentence it depends on. Second, поэтому can begin a new sentence in speech, which is common in conversation. Recognizing the structural difference is more reliable than memorizing a translation pair. One more practical point follows from the same structure. Because потому что introduces a dependent clause, it cannot open a sentence on its own the way поэтому can, so a beginner who wants to lead with the reason should restructure the sentence rather than place потому что first. Поэтому, by contrast, sits comfortably at the start of a spoken sentence, which is one reason it appears so often in explanations and briefings.
depth.secondExample: Use a cause with an emotional consequence: я люблю эту книгу, потому что она честная (I love this book because it is honest). Then reverse it: эта книга честная, поэтому я её люблю (this book is honest, therefore I love it). The same two clauses are now connected from the other direction.
depth.mistake: The commonest error is using потому что to introduce a result, which produces a sentence that names a consequence as though it were a reason. A second is using потому что and поэтому together in one sentence to mark the same relationship twice. A third is mishearing the compressed spoken form and writing it as two unconnected words, which then looks like a different construction.
depth.application: Write four pairs of sentences about your own week, expressing each pair once with потому что and once with поэтому, and swap the clause order each time. Then mark in each sentence whether the cause or the result comes first, and confirm the connector matches.
depth.summary: Потому что introduces a reason and поэтому introduces a result. Both describe the same relationship, and you may begin with either end as long as the connector matches.

lessons.title: When and if: когда and если
lessons.explanation: Когда (kag-DA, when) and если (YES-lee, if) both open a dependent clause, but they differ in what they promise about reality. Когда presents the event as something that happens or happened, and asks only about timing: когда я приду, я позвоню (kag-DA ya pree-DOO ya pa-zva-NYOO, when I arrive, I will call). Если presents the event as something that may or may not happen: если я приду, я позвоню (YES-lee ya pree-DOO ya pa-zva-NYOO, if I come, I will call). The words are close in sound and completely different in commitment. This distinction is the Russian counterpart of the difference between when and if in English, but Russian enforces it more consistently, so a beginner who says когда while meaning если suggests that the event is already certain. Notice how the two clauses interact with future time. When the main clause refers to the future, the clause with когда or если normally uses a present tense form rather than a future form: когда я приду, я позвоню. This is a real structural rule and one of the most useful adjustments a learner can make, because it removes an entire class of future tense errors.
lessons.example: A friend asks about your plan. You answer with an uncertain condition: если будет время, я поеду (YES-lee BOO-deet VRYE-mee-ya ya pa-YE-doo, if there is time, I will go). The word если tells your friend the trip is not settled. Later the plan firms up and you say: когда я поеду, я куплю билет (kag-DA ya pa-YE-doo ya koop-LYOO bee-LYET, when I go, I will buy a ticket). You have not changed the trip itself. You have changed your commitment to it, and Russian records that change in one word.
lessons.question: Why is когда я поеду, я куплю билет different in meaning from если я поеду, я куплю билет?
lessons.answer: Когда presents the trip as something that will happen and asks only about timing. Если presents it as possible rather than certain. The second sentence leaves open whether the trip happens at all.
lessons.distractor: There is no real difference in meaning; the two words are interchangeable variants of the same idea.
lessons.correction: They are not interchangeable. Если marks a genuine condition, which means the event might not occur. Когда marks a time, which presupposes the event occurs. A listener hearing когда understands that you consider the trip settled. Choosing когда when you mean если therefore overstates your certainty, which in a business or medical context can be a serious misunderstanding.

depth.definitions: A conditional clause states a condition that must hold for the main clause to be true. A temporal clause states a time at which the main clause holds. A presupposition is something a sentence takes for granted rather than asserts.
depth.mechanism: Если introduces a condition, so the main clause depends on whether the condition is met. Когда introduces a time reference, so the main clause is assumed to happen and only its moment is in question. That presupposition is the core difference and it survives translation. The tense rule follows from how Russian handles future reference in dependent clauses: rather than using a future form twice, Russian marks futurity once, in the main clause, and leaves the dependent clause in a present form.
depth.secondExample: Compare a question and a condition about the same person. Когда он придёт, мы начнём (kag-DA on pree-DYOT my NAch-nyom, when he arrives, we will begin) treats his arrival as certain and only waits for it. Если он придёт, мы начнём (YES-lee on pree-DYOT my NAch-nyom, if he arrives, we will begin) admits that he may not come at all.
depth.mistake: The most common error is using когда for a genuine condition, which overstates certainty. A second is putting a future form in the dependent clause, producing phrases like когда я буду приду. A third is confusing если with ли, the particle used for yes-or-no indirect questions, as in я не знаю, придёт ли он (I do not know whether he will come).
depth.application: Write four sentence pairs about your coming week, one member of each pair using когда and one using если, keeping both clauses otherwise identical. Then state for each pair which version asserts the event and which leaves it open, and note how the difference would sound to a listener.
depth.summary: Когда treats the event as real and asks about timing, while если treats it as possible. In future sentences the dependent clause keeps a present form.

lessons.title: Reporting what someone said
lessons.explanation: Russian reports speech with что (shto, that) after a verb of saying, thinking, or knowing: он сказал, что он занят (on ska-ZAL shta on ZA-nyat, he said that he is busy). Two details make this easier than it looks. First, Russian writes a comma before что, which visually separates the two clauses and helps you read long sentences. Second, Russian does not shift the tense backward the way English often does. English moves he is busy to he was busy when reporting it. Russian leaves the reported clause in the tense of the original statement: он сказал, что он занят. He said it, and the state described is still the one he asserted. This is a genuine simplification, and it removes one of the hardest habits a learner carries over from English. For yes-or-no questions, Russian uses the particle ли (lee) instead of что: он спросил, придёт ли она (on spra-SEEL pree-DYOT lee a-NA, he asked whether she would come). Note that what can be either the conjunction that or the question word what depending on the structure, and the two uses differ in intonation and in whether a comma precedes them.
lessons.example: You are passing on a message at work. A colleague told you she is busy until Friday. You report: она сказала, что она занята до пятницы. Notice that занята stayed in the present, because that is how she stated her situation. Then you report her question: она спросила, будет ли она нужна в пятницу (a-NA spra-SEE-la BOO-deet lee a-NA noozh-NA v PYAT-nee-tsoo, she asked whether she would be needed on Friday). Two verbs of reporting, two different connectors, because one introduced a statement and the other introduced a question.
lessons.question: Why does Russian say он сказал, что он занят rather than shifting to a past form as English does?
lessons.answer: Because Russian does not require tense backshift. The reported clause keeps the tense of the original statement, while English often moves it back one step.
lessons.distractor: Because Russian has no past tense for describing states, so занят is the only available form.
lessons.correction: Russian certainly has a past tense. The reason is not a gap in the language but a difference in convention. Russian reports the content of a statement as it was made, without the optional backshift English uses. Заниматься would give a past form like был занят (was busy) if you wanted to report a state that has ended, and that choice carries meaning rather than being grammatically forced.

depth.definitions: Indirect speech reports what someone said without quoting it directly. Direct speech reproduces the original words. Backshift is the English habit of moving a reported verb one tense into the past.
depth.mechanism: Что joins the reporting verb to the reported clause and behaves as a subordinating conjunction, so the clause after it is dependent. Ли marks an indirect yes-or-no question and sits after the word being questioned, which is usually the verb: придёт ли она. Because ли is a particle rather than a conjunction, its position inside the clause matters, and moving it changes which element is being asked about. That is why learners who translate whether word for word produce sentences that sound wrong. There is also a useful contrast with direct speech. When you quote someone's exact words, Russian typically introduces the quotation with a dash rather than with что, and the quoted sentence keeps its own capital letter and punctuation. Indirect reporting, by contrast, folds the content into a single sentence with a comma and a lowercase continuation. Choosing between the two is a register decision rather than a grammatical one, and mixing them in one sentence produces the kind of error that reads as a translation artifact.
depth.secondExample: Report a thought rather than a statement: я думаю, что это хорошая идея (ya DOO-ma-yoo shta EH-ta ha-RO-sha-ya ee-DYE-ya, I think that this is a good idea). Now report an uncertainty: я не знаю, хорошая ли это идея (ya nye ZNA-yoo ha-RO-sha-ya lee EH-ta ee-DYE-ya, I do not know whether this is a good idea). The conjunction что states content; the particle ли states a question.
depth.mistake: The most frequent error is backshifting the reported clause out of habit, producing a past form where Russian keeps the present. A second is omitting the comma before что, which makes long sentences harder to parse. A third is using что for an indirect question instead of ли.
depth.application: Report five things you heard or thought today, three as statements with что and two as questions with ли. Then rewrite each statement as a direct report and note which forms changed. Model: он сказал, что опоздает, and its question counterpart он спросил, опоздает ли он.
depth.summary: Russian reports statements with что and indirect questions with ли, and it does not shift the reported tense backward the way English often does.

lessons.title: A connected account: time markers and sequence
lessons.explanation: This lesson builds the skill the whole level has been preparing: speaking in connected paragraphs rather than isolated sentences. Russian organises a narrative with time markers that act like signposts. Сначала (sna-CHA-la, at first) opens. Потом (pa-TOM, then) continues. Затем (za-TYEM, after that) continues in a slightly more formal register. Наконец (na-ka-NYETS, finally) closes. Alongside these you will use clock and calendar words such as утром (OOT-ram, in the morning), вечером (VYE-chee-ram, in the evening), вчера (fchee-RA, yesterday), and через час (CHYE-ryes chas, in an hour). Two habits hold a Russian narrative together. First, place the time marker early in the sentence, which signals the frame before the details arrive. Second, use the pairing of и and а that you studied earlier to move between your own actions and someone else's, rather than repeating и for everything. A short account in this style sounds like this: сначала я работал, потом пошёл домой, а вечером читал книгу (sna-CHA-la ya ra-BO-tal pa-TOM pa-SHYOL da-MOY a VYE-chee-ram chee-TAL KNEE-goo, at first I worked, then I went home, and in the evening I read a book). Four clauses, four signposts, one continuous story.
lessons.example: You are telling a friend about yesterday. You say: вчера утром я ходил в магазин (fchee-RA OOT-ram ya ha-DEEL v ma-ga-ZEEN, yesterday morning I went to the shop). Then you keep going: потом я готовил обед, а вечером читал (pa-TOM ya ga-TO-veel a-BYET a VYE-chee-ram chee-TAL, then I cooked lunch, and in the evening I read). Finally you close the account: наконец я лёг спать (na-ka-NYETS ya lyog spat, finally I went to bed). Each sentence carries its own signpost, so your listener always knows where in the story they are.
lessons.question: Why does a Russian narrative often put the time marker at the beginning of the sentence rather than at the end?
lessons.answer: Because the time marker frames the whole clause. Putting it first tells the listener when the action happened before they process the details, and it lets the word order of the rest of the clause stay flexible.
lessons.distractor: Because Russian grammar forbids placing a time expression at the end of a sentence.
lessons.correction: Russian does not forbid it. Time expressions can move, and you will hear them in other positions. The reason to put them first is informational, not grammatical. Russian organises word order around what is already known and what is new, and the time frame is usually shared context, so it comes early. The new or emphasised material then lands at the end, which is the same instinct that guides English rhythm.

depth.definitions: A discourse marker is a word or phrase that organises a text rather than adding facts, such as first, then, finally. Information structure is the arrangement of a sentence according to what the listener already knows and what is new.
depth.mechanism: Connected speech works by alternation. A signpost establishes the frame, the clause then delivers one event, and the next signpost opens a new frame. Because each sentence is self-locating, a listener who loses one clause can rejoin at the next signpost rather than losing the thread. This is why learners who can produce accurate single sentences still sound incoherent: they have the grammar but not the signposts. Adding four or five discourse markers to your active vocabulary improves comprehension more than adding twenty nouns. Sequencing also interacts with verb aspect, because a completed event and a repeated or ongoing event call for different verb forms. For now, the safe habit is to attach one clear event to each signpost rather than packing several events into one clause, which keeps the aspect decision simple and the sequence easy for a listener to follow.
depth.secondExample: Compare a list of unconnected sentences with a connected account. Unconnected: я работал. Я пошёл домой. Я читал. Connected: сначала я работал, потом пошёл домой, а вечером читал. The facts are identical. Only the second version is a story, because the speaker has told you how the pieces relate in time.
depth.mistake: The most common error is producing accurate sentences with no discourse markers, which sounds clipped and forces the listener to infer sequence. A second is repeating и between every clause, which flattens the contrast between actions and makes the account monotonous. A third is putting every time marker in the same position regardless of what is shared knowledge, which produces sentences that are grammatical but hard to follow.
depth.application: Write a six sentence account of yesterday using at least four different time markers, one contrast with а, and one closing marker. Read it aloud twice, then record yourself once and listen for whether each sentence tells the listener where in the story they are. Model opening: сначала я встал рано, потом позавтракал.
depth.summary: A connected account needs signposts, not just correct sentences. Place time markers early, vary your connectors, and close the sequence clearly.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between потому что and поэтому in terms of what follows each one?
questions.answer: Потому что introduces a reason, and поэтому introduces a result. The clause after each connector states a different end of the same relationship.
questions.distractor: They are two spellings of the same word, and either may introduce either a reason or a result.
questions.correction: The two differ in direction. Потому что points backward to a cause that explains what was just said. Поэтому points forward to a consequence. Swapping them reverses the logic of the sentence even though both words sound similar.

questions.prompt: You are not sure whether your friend will come to an event. Should you say когда он придёт or если он придёт, and why?
questions.answer: Если он придёт, because the arrival is possible rather than certain. Когда would presuppose that he is definitely coming.
questions.distractor: Когда он придёт, because когда is the standard connector for any future event.
questions.correction: Когда presupposes that the event will happen and asks only about its timing. Since the arrival is genuinely uncertain, если is required. Using когда would tell your friend you already consider his attendance settled.

questions.prompt: In a sentence where the main clause is in the future, what form does the dependent clause after когда or если take, and why?
questions.answer: A present tense form. Russian marks futurity once, in the main clause, rather than using a future form in both clauses.
questions.distractor: A future tense form, because both clauses must agree in tense.
questions.correction: Russian does not repeat future marking across both clauses. The main clause carries the future sense, and the dependent clause stays in a present form, as in когда я приду, я позвоню. Putting a future form in the dependent clause produces phrases that a native speaker would not say.

questions.prompt: How does Russian report a yes-or-no question differently from a statement, and what word marks each?
questions.answer: Statements are reported with что, and yes-or-no questions are reported with the particle ли.
questions.distractor: Both are reported with что, and the difference is carried by intonation alone.
questions.correction: The conjunction что introduces reported statements, while the particle ли marks an indirect yes-or-no question. Ли sits after the word being questioned, usually the verb, so its position inside the clause carries meaning that intonation alone could not.

questions.prompt: Why can five grammatically correct sentences still fail to work as a spoken account?
questions.answer: Because accuracy is not the same as connection. Without discourse markers such as сначала, потом, and наконец, the listener cannot tell how the events relate in time.
questions.distractor: Because Russian requires at least one subordinate clause in every spoken account.
questions.correction: There is no such requirement. The problem is information structure rather than clause type. Signposts frame each sentence, so a listener who loses one clause can rejoin at the next marker. Without them, each sentence stands alone and the listener must reconstruct the sequence themselves.

questions.prompt: You say a new lamp and want the adjective to agree. Which form of новый is correct, and what rule decided it?
questions.answer: Новая, because лампа is feminine and the adjective copies the noun's gender.
questions.distractor: Новый, because adjectives keep their dictionary form before any noun.
questions.correction: The noun decides. Лампа is feminine, so the adjective takes the feminine ending. Agreement means the adjective carries the same gender, number, and case as its noun, which is also why a listener hears the gender twice.

questions.prompt: Which form of какой fits the question about a bag, and why does какой change at all while кто does not?
questions.answer: Какая, because сумка is feminine. Какой modifies a noun and so must agree with it, while кто replaces a person outright and has no noun to copy.
questions.distractor: Какой, because question words never change and only the noun changes.
questions.correction: Question words that modify a noun behave like adjectives and inflect. Какой belongs to that group, so it agrees with the noun being asked about. Кто and что stand in for the noun itself, so there is nothing for them to agree with.

questions.prompt: A learner writes эта книга более интереснее. Name the fault and give both correct alternatives.
questions.answer: The comparison is marked twice. Correct forms are эта книга более интересная and эта книга интереснее.
questions.distractor: Более may not be used with adjectives, so the phrase should be эта книга очень интереснее.
questions.correction: Более does combine with adjectives. The fault is using it together with the short comparative ending -ее, which marks the same comparison a second time. Choose the analytical form, более plus the full adjective, or the short form alone.

questions.prompt: Explain why самый больше всех is not standard, and give one correct superlative structure for a noun.
questions.answer: It combines the самый construction with a comparative and marks the ranking twice. A correct structure is самый большой, where самый agrees with the noun.
questions.distractor: It is not standard because самый cannot appear before an adjective of quantity.
questions.correction: Самый combines with plain adjectives, not with comparatives. Ranking a noun calls for самый plus an agreeing plain adjective. Ranking an action or a person against a group calls for a comparative plus всех. The two structures are alternatives.

questions.prompt: Write the phrases for two tables and five tables and explain why the noun form differs.
questions.answer: Два стола uses the genitive singular, and пять столов uses the genitive plural, because the numeral boundary falls between four and five.
questions.distractor: Both use the nominative plural, since any count above one makes the noun plural in Russian.
questions.correction: Russian splits the numerals into two patterns. Two, three, and four behave with the noun and take the genitive singular. Five and above behave as nouns of quantity and take the genitive plural. The boundary sits exactly between four and five.

questions.prompt: What does the quantity word сколько require of the noun that follows it, and why?
questions.answer: The genitive. Quantity words express amount rather than a specific count, so the noun follows them in the genitive.
questions.distractor: The nominative, because сколько is a question word and nouns stay in the nominative after questions.
questions.correction: Quantity and question status are separate matters. Сколько, много, and мало all express amount, and amount in Russian governs the genitive. This is the same case that marks possession and absence.

questions.prompt: Choose between и, а, and но for the sentence I am tired but happy, and justify the choice.
questions.answer: Но, because the two qualities pull against each other and the sentence expresses contrast. И would present them as a simple list, and а would only set them side by side.
questions.distractor: И, because both qualities describe the same person and Russian joins statements about one subject with и.
questions.correction: И encodes addition without tension, so it would flatten the point of the sentence. А encodes juxtaposition, which is softer than a genuine contrast. Но marks a real tension between two statements, which is exactly what tired but happy expresses.

questions.prompt: A colleague says я заболел, поэтому не пришёл. Restate the same facts with the other connector, and label which clause is the cause.
questions.answer: Я не пришёл, потому что заболел. The cause is заболеть, getting ill, and it now follows the connector.
questions.distractor: Я заболел, потому что не пришёл. The cause is not coming, and it follows the connector.
questions.correction: Reversing the connectors also reverses the logic. In the original, getting ill is the cause and not coming is the result. When restated with потому что, the cause still comes after the connector, so it must be the illness rather than the absence.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between когда он придёт, мы начнём and если он придёт, мы начнём.
questions.answer: Когда treats his arrival as certain and waits only for the moment. Если treats it as possible, leaving open whether he arrives at all.
questions.distractor: They mean the same thing, since both sentences describe a future arrival followed by a beginning.
questions.correction: The events described are identical, but the presuppositions differ. Когда takes the arrival for granted and asks about timing. Если makes the arrival a condition that may fail. In a business or clinical setting, that difference in certainty can change how a commitment is understood.

questions.prompt: How would you report the question will she come, and why does что not work here?
questions.answer: With ли: он спросил, придёт ли она. Что introduces reported statements, not indirect yes-or-no questions.
questions.distractor: With что: он спросил, что придёт она. Что covers both statements and questions.
questions.correction: Что reports the content of a statement. An indirect yes-or-no question needs the particle ли, which attaches after the word being questioned. Using что here would make the sentence read as though she announced her arrival rather than being asked about it.

questions.prompt: Does Russian shift a reported statement one tense back, as English often does? Explain with an example.
questions.answer: No. Russian keeps the tense of the original statement, as in он сказал, что он занят, where the present form remains even though the reporting verb is past.
questions.distractor: Yes. Russian requires the reported clause to move one tense into the past, so занят becomes был занят automatically.
questions.correction: Russian does not impose backshift. The reported clause keeps the tense in which the statement was made, and occupied or not is a meaning choice rather than a grammatical requirement. This removes a rule that learners often carry over from English.

questions.prompt: Your five sentences are each correct but the account sounds disjointed. What is missing, and how would you repair it?
questions.answer: Discourse markers. Adding signposts such as сначала, потом, а вечером, and наконец frames each sentence so the listener can follow the sequence.
questions.distractor: Subordinate clauses. Every sentence in a spoken account needs at least one dependent clause to connect it to the next.
questions.correction: Connection in speech comes from markers that organise the text, not from clause type. Signposts establish the frame before the details arrive, which also lets word order stay flexible. Adding four or five of them to active vocabulary improves comprehension more than adding many new nouns.
